entities.name: Temple of All Religions
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Temple of All Religions (Russian: Храм всех религий, Khram vsekh religiy) in Kazan, Russia — an unusual architectural complex built by the private citizen Ildar Khanov (an artist and healer, 1940-2013) beginning in 1992 on his own initiative and funded by his artwork sales and donations — is a unique contemporary sacred building that incorporates architectural elements of 16 world religions (including Islam, Christianity, Judaism, Buddhism, Hinduism, and others) into a single eclectic structure, expressing an individual vision of religious unity and human spiritual harmony.

Ildar Khanov's Temple of All Religions is exceptional in the history of sacred architecture: unlike nearly all historic religious buildings (which are built by institutions to serve a specific faith community), Kazan's temple was a personal artistic project by a single individual seeking to create a physical statement of inter-religious harmony. Kazan — where Russian Orthodox Christianity meets Tatar Islamic culture — is geographically appropriate for such a statement; the city has been a meeting point of Slavic and Turkic cultures since the Russian conquest of the Kazan Khanate in 1552.

The building, still under construction at Khanov's 2013 death and continued by family members, incorporates a Russian Orthodox dome, Islamic crescent and minarets, Buddhist pagoda elements, Star of David windows, Hindu temple forms, and many other architectural religious symbols in a deliberately syncretic composition. It has no active congregation or ritual function — it serves primarily as a cultural and tourism site, and as a statement of one artist's vision of religious coexistence. In a region that has experienced religious conflict, its existence is historically notable.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Temple of All Religions — a unique private architectural statement of inter-religious harmony incorporating 16 faith traditions in post-Soviet Kazan, built by a single artist's personal vision — is a historically distinctive example of individual sacred architecture and religious syncretism at the crossroads of Slavic and Islamic cultures.
